clue.text: Job application, getting rent freezes with it

parts.note: an app is short for an application, as on a phone
taken as printed
to ice is to freeze
someone with it is fashionable, hip

explanation.surface: A job-seeker filling in a form while worrying that the rent is frozen.
explanation.walkthrough: "Job application" reads as one phrase; split it, and application is the first piece of wordplay while Job alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An apprenticeship is a job in which a trainee learns a trade.

clue.text: Country welcomed in dreamer — I capitalized!

indicators.note: the answer is taken in by the words that follow, sitting inside them

parts.note: the letters run from the fourth of dreamer, through I, into the start of capitalized

explanation.surface: A dreamer boasting of having cashed in, the American dream.
explanation.walkthrough: dre-AMER I CA-pitalized. The dash and the capitalist boast point to the American dream, which is a hint at the answer sitting right there in the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In everyday speech the name of the continent is used for the single country, the United States, as in 'made in America'.

clue.text: Alien from Ancient Rome

definitions.meaning: the surface reading: a creature from another world; the setter's reading: a person who is not welcome
the phrase for such a person is Latin, the language of Ancient Rome

explanation.walkthrough: "Alien" suggests a creature from space; here it is an unwelcome outsider, described by a Latin phrase, hence from Ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: A persona non grata is a person not welcome, an outsider, and the phrase is Latin.

clue.text: Number beginning to elevate skywards? Not these

definitions.text: Number beginning to elevate skywards? Not these

indicators.note: skywards in a down clue means written upwards, so the letters read in reverse

parts.note: a sum is a number

indicators.note: beginning to takes the first letter of elevate

explanation.surface: A number of creatures that will never get off the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer: emus are flightless, so they are not things that rise skywards.
explanation.definitionFit: Emus are large flightless Australian birds, so they never take to the sky.

clue.text: Digital protection needs to speed up

parts.note: taken as printed

indicators.note: in a down answer, up means the letters read from the bottom

parts.note: pace is speed; read upward it becomes ECAP

explanation.surface: Online security needs to get faster.
explanation.walkthrough: "Digital protection" reads as cyber security; digits are also toes, so it is protection for the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A toecap is the hard covering on the toe of a boot, protecting the digits.

clue.text: Registers report of wrongdoing in Prague?

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so what follows is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a wrongdoing in Prague would be a Czech sin

explanation.surface: Someone records an account of misconduct in the Czech capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Prague is the Czech capital, so its wrongdoing is a Czech sin, which said out loud is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotel guest who registers checks in.

clue.text: County right to cut store's lease

parts.note: a store is a shop, plus the S of 's
R is short for right
to lease something is to hire it

explanation.surface: A council using its right to slash a shop's rent.
explanation.walkthrough: SHROPSHIRE is an English county on the Welsh border.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Shropshire is one of the English counties, rural and bordering Wales.

clue.text: Troublesome closing of public toilets?

definitions.meaning: the plain sense: causing people trouble

definitions.note: a cryptic description: in-convenience-ing, taking away conveniences
definitions.meaning: the setter's reading: public toilets are conveniences, so closing them takes people out of convenience

explanation.walkthrough: A public convenience is a public toilet, so shutting them is literally in-convenience-ing, and it troubles everyone who needs one.
explanation.definitionFit: Inconveniencing means causing trouble, as closing the public toilets would.

clue.text: Livingstone, say, converted any man or woman from Africa

parts.note: Ken Livingstone was the first Mayor of London, an example of a Ken

indicators.note: converted means changed, so the letters of any are rearranged

explanation.surface: The explorer Livingstone converting Africans to Christianity.
explanation.walkthrough: Livingstone suggests the missionary David, but it is the London politician Ken Livingstone.
explanation.definitionFit: A Kenyan is a native or citizen of Kenya, a country in East Africa.

clue.text: Coming from France?

definitions.meaning: the surface reading: arriving; the setter's reading: on the way
the phrase for on the way is borrowed from French

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as arriving from France; it means "coming", on the way, in a phrase that itself comes from French.
explanation.definitionFit: En route means on the way, so someone en route is coming.

clue.text: No protection for deaf motorists — that chap shows irritation

parts.note: deaf with its outer D and F stripped away
the RAC, Royal Automobile Club, is a British motorists' organisation
he is that chap

explanation.surface: Deaf drivers go without cover, and some man is annoyed about it.
explanation.walkthrough: "No protection" looks like insurance for motorists; it strips the outside letters off deaf.
explanation.definitionFit: Earache is informal for irritating talk, and so the irritation it causes.

clue.text: Hard element drive Father Christmas out of Santa Fe

definitions.meaning: a tough metal from the periodic table

definitions.text: Father Christmas out of Santa Fe
definitions.meaning: Father Christmas is Santa; take him away and Fe is left, a chemical symbol

explanation.surface: Expelling Santa Claus from the city of Santa Fe, a hard-hearted act.
explanation.walkthrough: Santa Fe is the capital of New Mexico; with Santa driven out, Fe is left, which is the chemical symbol for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses name the same metal: a hard element, and the one whose symbol is Fe, from Latin ferrum.

clue.text: Two Yanks cycling, one's front is hard, the other's soft but carrying on

parts.note: H is short for hard, as on pencils; it goes on the front of the first
YANK cycled becomes ANKY; this is the first of the two
p, piano, is soft in music; it fronts the second
the second YANK, cycled the same way

explanation.surface: Two Americans out on bikes, one hard at it, the other soft but pedalling on.
explanation.walkthrough: "Cycling" suggests bike riders; it rotates each YANK. H for hard is the pencil grade, and P for soft is piano in music.
explanation.definitionFit: Hanky-panky is carrying on, illicit or mischievous goings-on.

clue.text: Rival clubs in Paris, little to be revealed in changing room

indicators.note: the letters of room change their order
the word for little is given in French

parts.note: C is short for clubs, the card suit
room rearranged, split around PETIT
petit is French for little

explanation.surface: Rival Parisian football clubs, with a player's little secret exposed in the dressing room.
explanation.walkthrough: "Clubs" suggests football teams, but it is the card suit, C.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: anyone competing against you in a contest or market is your rival.

clue.text: Bowl over with one short leg and a runner

indicators.note: one short means the word is a single letter shy of full length, losing its last

parts.note: to bowl someone over is to amaze them
the last letter of the word for bowl over
in cricket the leg side is also called the on side

explanation.surface: A cricket picture: a bowler, a fielder at short leg and a batter running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowl', 'short leg' and 'runner' all look like cricket terms (short leg is a fielding position close to the batter), but short belongs with one and leg is the cricket side.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is said to run, so in crosswords a runner can be a river, and the Amazon is the great South American one.

clue.text: Figure of 'The Genie set free'

indicators.note: letters set free break out of their order

parts.note: the fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A figure from a story called The Genie Set Free, as in Aladdin.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make "The Genie set free" look like a title; it is the fodder and its instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: In crosswords 'figure' usually means a number, here the one after seventeen.

clue.text: One has a ding-dong to get admission

definitions.meaning: the surface reading: someone has a row; the setter's reading: the thing goes ding-dong
a visitor rings it to be let in

explanation.walkthrough: A ding-dong is a row or fight; it is also the sound of a doorbell, which one rings to be let in.
explanation.definitionFit: A doorbell goes ding-dong when a visitor wants to be let in.

clue.text: Discount ring sent back twice

indicators.note: twice asks for the reversed word to be written two times
sent back means returned, so the ring word is read backwards

parts.note: a hoop is a ring

explanation.surface: A ring returned to the shop is twice marked down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' turns HOOP into POOH; 'twice' doubles it.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismiss an idea scornfully is to discount it, the verb sense of this reduplicated word.

clue.text: Leave grub youngster polished off

parts.note: a pup is a young animal
to polish off food is to eat it all

explanation.surface: Food left over that a child gobbled up.
explanation.walkthrough: "Leave grub" reads as leftover food; grub is also a larva, and it leaves that stage when it turns into a pupa.
explanation.definitionFit: To pupate is to turn from a larva into a pupa, leaving the grub stage behind.

clue.text: Causes a ferment in speech that turns blue?

definitions.note: the question mark allows the verb: a fruit or skin that bruises goes blue

indicators.note: in speech means the word is heard, not read

parts.note: brewing beer sets it fermenting

explanation.surface: Heated talk that makes the air blue with swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: "Turns blue" hints at bad language; it is the colour of a bruise.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin that bruises goes blue, and the question mark signals the loose fit.

clue.text: Person in the ascendant, Iron Throne-holder?

indicators.note: something in the ascendant is rising, and in a down answer rising letters read from the bottom upward

parts.note: me is a pronoun in the first person, the grammatical sense of person; climbing, it becomes EM
to iron clothes is to press them

explanation.surface: A rising figure who sits on the Iron Throne, as in Game of Thrones.
explanation.walkthrough: "Iron Throne" reads as one phrase from Game of Thrones; split it, and Iron is a verb in the wordplay while Throne-holder alone defines. Person is grammatical: ME is first person.
explanation.definitionFit: An empress is a female sovereign who rules an empire and occupies its throne, the question mark marking a playful periphrasis.

clue.text: Begin play, Shakespeare's Hamle?

definitions.meaning: the golf sense: to start a round by driving from the peg

definitions.note: a cryptic description: the title with its last letter gone
definitions.meaning: the play's title is missing its final letter, the twentieth of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A theatre direction to start a Shakespeare play, with a typo in the title.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamle is Hamlet with the T taken off, so it is T off, spelt out as the golf term. The question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfing idiom: every round starts with a drive from the tee, so to begin play is to tee off.

clue.text: Thriller, where words are written by famous artist

parts.note: words are written on a page
J. M. W. Turner, the English painter

explanation.surface: A thriller whose text was written by a famous painter.
explanation.walkthrough: "By" is the link that puts TURNER beside PAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A page-turner is a gripping book, like a thriller that keeps you reading.

clue.text: Lose rag, knocking pots over

indicators.note: knocking the pots over turns them upside down

parts.note: pans are cooking pots

explanation.surface: Someone losing their temper and knocking over the pots in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: To lose your rag is British slang for losing your temper. "Over" belongs with knocking: knocked over, the pans are turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: To snap is to lose your temper suddenly.

clue.text: What Greek eats flipping salt beefy sandwiches in slices?

indicators.note: flipping turns the kept letters round
a sandwich alternates layers, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters, which are then flipped

explanation.surface: A question about Greek food: salt beef sandwiches, sliced.
explanation.walkthrough: sAlTbEeFy gives ATEF, flipped to FETA. Salt beef is a deli favourite, so the sandwiches look like the food; they are the instruction to take alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Feta is the salty Greek cheese, a staple of Greek eating.

clue.text: Taste of Moscato Asti exquisite for light lunch?

indicators.note: a taste is only a small part of the phrase

parts.note: the letters start at the end of Moscato, take all of Asti and the first of exquisite

explanation.surface: Sipping an Italian sparkling wine with a light lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: mosca-TO ASTI E-xquisite. A toastie is British for a toasted sandwich.
explanation.definitionFit: A toastie is a toasted sandwich, a typical light lunch.

clue.text: Previous expansion of IT?

indicators.note: each letter of IT is expanded into the word it abbreviates

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one, expanded to the full word
T is the standard abbreviation for time, expanded to the full word

explanation.surface: Past growth in the information technology sector.
explanation.walkthrough: IT suggests information technology; the expansion is spelling out each letter as the word it stands for.
explanation.definitionFit: One-time means former or previous, as in a one-time champion.

clue.text: Bear hugs for all represented fun (or not!)

indicators.note: the letters are presented again in a new form

parts.note: the fodder, fourteen letters

explanation.surface: Bear hugs for everyone, which some people enjoy and some don't.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket covers the phrase's usual ironic use: "he's a barrel of laughs" often means he is no fun at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrel of laughs is great fun, though the phrase is usually said sarcastically.
